To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the plasma carcinoembryogenic antigen (CEA) is elevated in the serum of 80% of patients with brain metastasis; 2) the CEA is elevated in 90% of patients with primary brain tumors and is elevated in the majority of patients who have had brain irradiation; and 3) the plasma CEA reflects the clinical course of the intracranial metastases and may be useful as an indicator of tumor control, response to radiation,

1) CEA is a useful marker in patients with brain metastasis; 2) CEA is elevated in the presence of brain metastasis; and 3) CEA levels correlate with the extent and response to treatment of brain metastases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method for the determination of CEA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
the development of a new method of producing and characterizing the surface of a solid material.
the use of plasma carcinoembryonicionic antigen (CEA) as a diagnostic tool in the management of brain tumors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CEA is a marker of the extent of disease, and that its usefulness as a marker for the response to therapy remains to be established.
the CEA test is a valuable adjunct to other laboratory tests and clinical observations in the diagnosis and management of cancer patients.

the plasma carcinoembryoniconic antigen is a useful tumor marker in patients with colorectal cancer and that its usefulness is enhanced when it is combined with a careful history and physical examination, with appropriate radiographic evaluation, and with a search for other tumor markers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the plasma CEA should be measured at regular intervals in patients with known brain metastases.
plasma CEA is an indicator of the presence of cerebral metastases in patients with elevated plasma CEA and is an indicator of response to therapy in patients with cerebral metastases.
the plasma carcinoembrynonic antigen is an important tumor marker in the management of patients with brain metastasis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CEA is an indicator of brain metastases and that a search to determine the cause of an elevated plasma CEA should include a search of the central nervous system.
the use of plasma CEA in the management of patients with brain metastasis is not only feasible, but can provide valuable information about disease status.
the CEA is a useful tumor marker in the setting of metastatic brain disease.
